card.hook: Here's the surprise: the grand stone front you're staring at is mostly 19th century, yet the Roman hot spring underneath it is still rising. Bath has been showing off for a very long time.
card.stand_here: Stand near Kingston Parade, right where the phone icon sits on the map, which is at the subject itself. Face the Grand Pump Room front on Abbey Church Yard, then step back a little so the Pump Room and the entrance building fit together.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x if you're close and want the whole front in one go, and 1x for the general view. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the columns, the pediment and the curve of the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the four columns up with the vertical lines so the building stands up straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon, when there are usually fewer people in front of the building. Wait a moment for a clear gap if someone wanders through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to Abbey Churchyard, on the square just outside Bath Abbey, and stand so the Roman Baths entrance is behind you with the Abbey beside it. Use the front camera at 0.5x to squeeze it all in. If the Christmas tree is up, it makes a cheerful extra, but it may not be there outside the festive season.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across Abbey Churchyard from the Roman Baths entrance while you stand near the entrance, so you and the whole entrance front fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Hand-held phones are welcome for personal photos around the site, and selfie sticks are allowed if you use them with care around other visitors. The original Roman paving is uneven, worn and sometimes slippery, so watch your feet while you pose. Check the official site for any rules on photography indoors.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a close-up of a single Corinthian column, and see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: A temple was built here between 60 and 70 AD, and the Roman town of Aquae Sulis grew up around it. The Grand Pump Room was finished in 1799, and the visitor entrance is an 1897 concert hall with a glass-domed centre. You can tour the baths and museum, but you can't get into the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Kingston Parade, right where the phone icon sits on the map, which is at the subject itself. Face the Grand Pump Room front on Abbey Church Yard, then step back a little so the Pump Room and the entrance building fit together.

card.hook: A glass cube dropped into a street of honey-coloured Georgian stone shouldn't work, but in Bath it really does. The best bit is where old meets new.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public streets around the spa, using the phone icon on the map (it marks the centre of the building) as your reference. Pick a spot where the whole glass cube fits in your frame, with a slice of the Georgian stone beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole cube in. If the street is too narrow to step back, tap 0.5x. For a second shot, go to 2x (or 5x if your phone has it) and aim at the join between the glass and the stone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the cube's edges with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean, and keep your phone upright.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the stone. Glass reflections tend to be clearest on bright but not harsh days. At dusk the lit-up glass glows against the darkening sky, so try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the cobbled Hot Bath Street, near the Thermae end, and turn so the spa building is behind you. Use your front camera (and 0.5x if your phone offers it) so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand further back up the cobbled street, away from the spa end, while you stand near the Thermae end so the whole building fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Take your photos outside the building, from the public streets. Phones aren't allowed inside the spa, and please don't photograph people inside or on the rooftop.
card.challenge: Find the reflection in the glass where the older buildings show up as soft shapes, and snap it before anyone walks through your shot.
card.good_to_know: Thermae Bath Spa reopened in 2006, ending a 28-year period when bathing in the city's hot spring water wasn't allowed. The water comes from the only naturally hot, mineral-rich springs in the UK, and the council has been its guardian under a royal charter of 1590. The glass cube is the New Royal Bath, designed by Grimshaw Architects, and it sits beside the grade I listed Georgian Cross Bath.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public streets around the spa, using the phone icon on the map (it marks the centre of the building) as your reference. Pick a spot where the whole glass cube fits in your frame, with a slice of the Georgian stone beside it.

card.hook: Look up at the front of Bath Abbey and you'll spot tiny stone angels climbing two ladders to the sky. Most people snap the whole façade and walk right past them.
card.stand_here: Stand in Abbey Churchyard, right in front of the Abbey's main west entrance, and face the Abbey. The Abbey is to the east of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole west front. If you can't step back far enough, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the angels and the window details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the edges of the towers up with the vertical lines, so the Abbey stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when there are fewer people in the square. The west front is likely to catch the light in the afternoon and evening.
card.selfie_here: Try Abbey Churchyard just outside the Abbey doors. Use your front camera, stand with the Abbey behind you, and step back or use 0.5x if you want the whole façade in. At Christmas there's a giant fir tree here that can sit in the shot too, but it's seasonal. York Street has the Abbey in the background framed by an arch, but it's not a proven selfie spot, so check it when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand a little way along Church Street, with the small fudge shop in the foreground of their frame, while you pose with the Abbey behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the Abbey is an active place of worship. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or behaviour guidance.
card.challenge: Can you find the angels on both stone ladders and get one of them sharp in your frame?
card.good_to_know: The church was founded in the 7th century, rebuilt in the 12th and 16th centuries, and restored by Sir George Gilbert Scott in the 1860s. It's Perpendicular Gothic, which means tall windows and strong vertical lines. Inside it's famous for its fan vaulting, and it still seats up to 1,200 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Abbey Churchyard, right in front of the Abbey's main west entrance, and face the Abbey. The Abbey is to the east of you.

card.hook: Here's the catch with the Royal Crescent: it's too big to fit in one photo unless you walk backwards across a lawn. Luckily, that's the fun part.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public lawn of Royal Victoria Park, directly in front of the Crescent and beyond the ha-ha. Then step back south across the lawn, staying on the park side, until both ends of the terrace fit. Face the Crescent with green grass in front of you.
card.zoom: Try zoom 0.5x if you can only get fairly close, or 1x from further back for straighter, more natural edges. Then use 2x to 5x to pick out the columns, lamp posts or front doors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the phone level so the rooflines don't lean, and let the lawn fill the bottom third of your picture.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the Bath stone looks warm and golden. Take your wide shot first, then a closer one of the columns and the ha-ha.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Great Lawn in front of the middle of the curve, well back from the terrace, so the whole sweep sits behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little low so the Crescent fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the path at the field's edge, where it meets the Marlborough Buildings side, while you stand on the lawn so they can fit the whole Crescent behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park lawn is public, but the grass directly in front of the houses may be for residents only, so stay on the park side of the ha-ha.
card.challenge: Get one shot where every column stands perfectly straight and the lawn fills the bottom third, and don't try to count all 114 columns.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Crescent is a row of 30 Georgian townhouses, designed by John Wood the Younger and built between 1767 and 1774. It's Grade I listed, and the stone front still looks much as it did when it was new. The curve is about 150 metres long, with 114 tall Ionic columns along the first floor.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public lawn of Royal Victoria Park, directly in front of the Crescent and beyond the ha-ha. Then step back south across the lawn, staying on the park side, until both ends of the terrace fit. Face the Crescent with green grass in front of you.

card.hook: Here's the odd thing about Pulteney Bridge: it's a whole little shopping street sitting on top of a river, and the river puts on a mini waterfall right in front of it. Yes, it's as photogenic as everyone says.
card.stand_here: Stand on Grand Parade, on the raised side above the river just south-west of the bridge. Face the bridge and look down toward its three arches and the weir, with the green hills rising behind the city.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the bridge and weir together. Switch to 0.5x if people or railings crowd your view, then try 2x for the arches and the temple-like middle. The bridge looks quite different wide and close, so take a few of each.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge on one of the lower lines, then tap the stonework and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the pale limestone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Daytime is the classic time for the bridge and weir together. If you'd like to see the bridge lit up in the evening, try North Parade Bridge.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the lawns and flower beds of Parade Gardens and stand with the bridge and weir behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the bridge over your shoulder. Check before you go whether there's a charge to get in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on Grand Parade, where the bridge and weir appear together in the classic daytime view, to take a photo of you with the bridge behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The riverside steps were reported dirty and slippery in February, so take care in wet weather. Buses and taxis still use the bridge, so keep clear of the roadway when you're shooting the shopfronts.
card.challenge: Get the three arches, the weir and the green hills all in one frame, then take the same shot at 1x and 2x and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Robert Adam designed Pulteney Bridge in a Palladian style, and it was finished by 1774 to link the city with new building land on the Bathwick side. It's one of only four bridges in the world with shops along the full length of both sides, and it's Grade I listed. The south face still shows Adam's hand, while the north side has been altered over the years.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Grand Parade, on the raised side above the river just south-west of the bridge. Face the bridge and look down toward its three arches and the weir, with the green hills rising behind the city.

card.hook: Stand at the corner of Queen Square and look up Gay Street: one long, tidy line of Georgian townhouses, with Jane Austen's place waiting at the far end.
card.stand_here: Stand in Queen Square at the top right corner, where Gay Street leads off. The Centre is a short walk north-east of here (about 1 minute on foot), so face north-east and look up the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole street and the terrace in the picture. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to bring the frontage closer without stepping into the traffic.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the buildings up with the vertical lines, so the terrace stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Try going early, since a narrow street like this is likely to be calmer then. The Centre is a ticketed attraction that recommends pre-booking, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Walk up to the porch at 40 Gay Street and stand beside the statue of Jane, so the Georgian townhouse entrance is behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 1x, or 0.5x if you want more of the facade. The figure may be moved or absent on some days, so check when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask your photographer to stand on the pavement opposite the doorway, on the street and not on the porch, so the entrance, statue and facade all fit in the frame while you stand by the door.
card.rules_and_safety: Respect any 'no photography' signs, especially inside historic buildings. Gay Street is narrow and busy, so look around before you step back to frame a shot.
card.challenge: Get the whole street dead straight against the gridlines from the Queen Square corner, then walk up and match it with a close-up of the door and the floral display.
card.good_to_know: Inside, a permanent exhibition tells the story of Jane Austen's time in Bath and how the city shaped her writing. There are also Regency Tea Rooms and a life-size wax figure of the author, unveiled in 2014. The Centre hosts the annual Jane Austen Festival, which has run since 2001, and its block (31–40 Gay Street) is Grade II listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Queen Square at the top right corner, where Gay Street leads off. The Centre is a short walk north-east of here (about 1 minute on foot), so face north-east and look up the street.

card.hook: Here's the honest bit: from up on the hill, The Circus is one small piece of a big Georgian view, not the star. That's what makes it a fun 'where does it all fit?' picture, with the Abbey and the Royal Crescent in the same frame.
card.stand_here: Head to Alexandra Park and find the benches on the high ground in the north-east corner. From there The Circus lies to the north, about 1.3 km away in a straight line, so face north over the rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole panorama, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pull The Circus and the Royal Crescent closer. If you go down to The Circus itself, zoom 0.5x helps fit in the curve of the terrace.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line, then tap the city and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning for clear air, or late afternoon when the light catches the crescents.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of The Circus among the central plane trees, use the front camera (try 0.5x) and let the ring of townhouses fill the frame behind you. Check the lawn is open to walk on first, as this spot is the closest match we found rather than a famous selfie corner.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the end of Bennett Street and shoot northwest across The Circus, with you posing in front of the houses (check the spot when you arrive).
card.rules_and_safety: The Circus is a public space, but the buildings are mainly homes, so be mindful of residents' privacy when you take pictures. Check whether the central lawn is open on the day.
card.challenge: Take a matching pair: the big view from the park, then the full sweep of the ring from the street, and see if you can spot the same trees in both.
card.good_to_know: The Circus was built between 1754 and 1768 and designed by John Wood the Elder. He made it 318 feet (97 m) across, echoing the size of Stonehenge, but died soon after the first stone was laid, so his son John Wood the Younger finished it. Look for the 525 small carved emblems in the frieze; the whole ring is Grade I listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Alexandra Park and find the benches on the high ground in the north-east corner. From there The Circus lies to the north, about 1.3 km away in a straight line, so face north over the rooftops.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing about the Holburne Museum: from the best spot, it's just a small building waiting at the end of a very long, very straight street. Let the street be the star and the museum be the punchline.
card.stand_here: Stand in Laura Place by the fountain, about 450 m from the museum, a short walk. Face down Great Pulteney Street so it runs straight away from you with the museum at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole street. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer. Skip 0.5x here, as it makes the museum look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the street's centre line in the middle, and keep your phone level so the building edges stay straight. Tap the museum, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter, with fewer people and cars on the street. Pick a time when sunlight falls on the buildings rather than shining straight at your phone.
card.selfie_here: Try the front forecourt of the Holburne Museum on Great Pulteney Street, with the main front of the building behind you. Use the front camera, and if your phone has a wider setting (0.5x), use it to fit more building over your shoulder. I couldn't confirm exactly which way to face, so check on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Laura Place end of Great Pulteney Street, then walk up the street with the museum at the far end behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Wait for a gap in people and traffic, and use your phone's zoom rather than stepping into the road. The museum is a visitor attraction, so check its official site for entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the street's lines point straight at the museum, like an arrow, with no cars in it. Bonus points if you beat the traffic!
card.good_to_know: The Holburne is a Grade I listed building. It was built as the Sydney Hotel, with the foundation stone laid in 1796, to serve the pleasure gardens. It became a museum in 1916 and was Bath's first public art gallery. A modern extension with ceramic cladding by Eric Parry Architects opened in 2011 at the rear.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Laura Place by the fountain, about 450 m from the museum, a short walk. Face down Great Pulteney Street so it runs straight away from you with the museum at the far end.

card.hook: Most people hit Bath Spa station with a suitcase in one hand and a phone in the other, and then walk straight past one of Brunel's prettiest buildings. Stop for a minute. It's worth a photo before you even reach the Roman Baths.
card.stand_here: Stand on Dorchester Street, in the street outside the frontage. Look towards the main station entrance, which is to the south-east, and let the street frame the building for you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole gabled front. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the building well away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the gables and the building's edges with them, so the straight lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go in daytime, when the stonework is evenly lit. People and vehicles will wander through, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest one later.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the station entrance, where the station sign is visible, and turn the front camera towards you. Switch to zoom 0.5x if your front camera has it, and tuck the sign and the Tudor-style frontage in behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Dorchester Street, west of the entrance, looking towards the station, while you stand in front of the entrance with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the frontage from the public street. It's a working station with ticket barriers, so check the official site before you go if you want to take photos on the platforms.
card.challenge: Find the gap above the main entrance where a clock should be, and get a shot that makes people say, 'Wait, where's the clock?'
card.good_to_know: Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the station for the Great Western Railway, and it opened on 31 August 1840. It's Grade II* listed, in an asymmetrical Tudor style with curving gables. The clock above the main entrance was taken down in 2022 over safety concerns about the Dutch gable, and as of April 2026 it hadn't been put back.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Dorchester Street, in the street outside the frontage. Look towards the main station entrance, which is to the south-east, and let the street frame the building for you.

card.hook: Royal Victoria Park was opened by an 11-year-old princess, and its quiet north-west corner is now a tidy patch of flower beds and trees. Start there and you'll have a good photo before you've even reached the big lawns.
card.stand_here: Stand inside Bath Botanical Gardens, in the north-west corner of Royal Victoria Park. You go in from the Crescent side. Face the flower beds and trees, with the wider park opening out to the south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for flower beds and tree-lined paths. Go to 0.5x for the wide lawns, or zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single bloom or bring the Crescent closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the flowers, then drag the slider a touch darker so the colours stay rich and bright petals don't wash out.
card.best_time: Spring, summer and autumn all bring colour, and autumn is said to be just as good as the flowering months. For the lake, early morning is the time to go.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of Park Lake with your back to the water, so the trees and sky are reflected behind you. Use the front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the scene in. Early morning is when the reflections are calmest. For a leafy backdrop, the little keepers' cottage near the Botanical Gardens sits among the trees and shrubs.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the lawn in front of the Royal Crescent, so they can fit the whole curve in the frame with you.
card.challenge: Find a bed of flowers, put it in the bottom third of your screen, and see if you can get the Crescent peeking out from behind the trees as well.
card.good_to_know: Princess Victoria opened the park in 1830, seven years before she became queen, and it was the first park to carry her name. It covers about 57 acres and is Grade I registered. The Botanical Gardens were laid out in 1887, and the Victoria Column, a stone obelisk about 10 m tall, went up in 1837 near the Marlborough Lane entrance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside Bath Botanical Gardens, in the north-west corner of Royal Victoria Park. You go in from the Crescent side. Face the flower beds and trees, with the wider park opening out to the south-east.

selfie_spots.why: The cottage sits in the trees and shrubs, so the park's greenery forms the background of the shot.

card.hook: Walk in under the colonnade and Bath shows off a bit: flower beds up front, then the river, the weir and Pulteney Bridge lined up behind like they're posing too.
card.stand_here: Stand under the colonnade along the western edge of Parade Gardens, about 250 yards east of Bath Abbey. Face across the gardens toward the river.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the beds, river and bridge in one shot. Go to 0.5x to squeeze in the colonnade and more lawn, then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the weir or Pulteney Bridge. Rest your phone against a column or the railing to keep it steady.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the river on the upper line and let the flower beds fill the bottom, with a column at the edge of the shot as a frame.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. The flower beds look best in the warmer months.
card.selfie_here: Try it under the colonnade on the western edge: use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the columns and the gardens behind you. Nobody has a famous selfie spot here, so take a couple and check which angle looks best.
card.ask_someone: Stand on North Parade Bridge and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the gardens and Pulteney Bridge in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry arrangements have changed over time and may involve a fee, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a bed of flowers sharp in front with the weir softly blurred behind it, and give yourself a point if a column frames the edge.
card.good_to_know: Parade Gardens is a grade II listed park, laid out in 1709 and first called St James's Park for visitors who came to take the waters. After the Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution was built in 1824, it was known as the Institution Gardens for a time. There's a cafe on site, and North Parade Bridge gives a higher, wider view down onto the gardens.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand under the colonnade along the western edge of Parade Gardens, about 250 yards east of Bath Abbey. Face across the gardens toward the river.

selfie_spots.why: It offers fine views of the River Avon and the weir, especially from the Italianate colonnade at the western end of the garden. Standing there and facing the water should put the gardens behind you, though no source describes a selfie from this spot.

card.hook: Jane Austen knew this place well enough to name it in two of her novels, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion. Today the show is the front: a row of columns and arched windows in that warm, creamy Bath stone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bennett Street, opposite the colonnaded north front by the Ballroom, and face south. From there you see the whole front straight on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the columns and windows keep their natural shape. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all in, try 0.5x and keep your phone level. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the columns and arched windows.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the front looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Bright overcast daylight or a clear morning gives even light on the stone. Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the pavement too.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and, if your phone has it, try 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in. Turn your back to the columns, tilt the phone up a little, and keep the building over your shoulder. Check first that the front isn't hidden behind hoardings.
card.rules_and_safety: The building is under renovation, so hoardings may partly screen the front. Check the official site before you go to see how much is visible. Keep an eye on traffic and other pedestrians while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Can you get a straight-on shot where the columns line up perfectly with the gridlines and no wonky walls sneak in?
card.good_to_know: John Wood the Younger designed the Assembly Rooms in 1769, and they opened with a grand ball in 1771. The ballroom is about 30 metres long, the largest Georgian interior in Bath. It was bombed and burnt out in the Second World War, then restored and reopened in 1963. It's now Grade I listed and owned by the National Trust.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bennett Street, opposite the colonnaded north front by the Ballroom, and face south. From there you see the whole front straight on.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the Bath Assembly Rooms behind them, or a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole building in frame. I have not added any place from memory. The closest candidates were rejected: the Hidden Stairs off George Street (The Chaos Diaries) are described as heading toward the Assembly Rooms, but the page does not say the building is in the background. The top of Broad Street (The Chaos Diaries) is described as looking down toward the city, which faces away from the building. Circus and Bennett Street appear only as access directions (Free City Guides; An Historian About Town), not as photo spots. Rules: the only photography guidance is from Airial, which says personal photography is generally permitted but should be checked for restrictions such as special exhibitions or flash bans. Airial also says a tripod 'might be beneficial' for low light, which is advice, not a rule, so I left it out. No selfie-stick or tripod rule was stated by any page. Safety: no page mentioned one. Sources consulted: thechaosdiaries.com/most-instagrammable-places-in-bath/, free-city-guides.com/bath/bath-assembly-rooms/, anhistorianabouttown.com/the-bath-assembly-rooms/, airial.travel (Bath Assembly Rooms 2025), nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/bath-bristol/bath-assembly-rooms. A local search of the square in front of the Assembly Rooms on Bennett Street, or of the Circus viewpoint, might find a spot, but nothing I found confirms one.

card.hook: Picture a street so wide and straight that it looks like someone drew it with a ruler, with a grand building plugging the far end like a cork. That's Great Pulteney Street, and it's over 300 m long and about 30 m wide, which makes it the widest and grandest street in Bath.
card.stand_here: Stand in Laura Place, the little square at the city end of the street, right by the fountain in the middle. Face along the street towards the Holburne Museum at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the full width of the street and the houses on both sides. Then try 1x for a more natural look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pull the Holburne Museum a bit closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the centre of the road up with the middle of the frame, and keep your phone upright so the houses don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in your shot. Take a few frames either way, because traffic and passers-by change from one shot to the next.
card.selfie_here: Walk down to the Holburne Museum at the far end and stand in front of its grand façade, so the street runs away behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone so the museum fills the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the Laura Place fountain and shoot back up the street, while you stand in the foreground with the Holburne Museum small in the distance behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no general restrictions on personal photography on the street, but be mindful of privacy when you photograph people. If you plan to go inside the Holburne Museum, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Walk the street and hunt for the little differences: door heights, balconies and painted house numbers. Then snap the spot where number 13 should be and see if you can find it.
card.good_to_know: Thomas Baldwin designed the street and it was finished in 1789, but he only designed the façades. Individual owners built the houses behind them, so the street looks uniform outside but differs inside. The fountain in Laura Place replaced a much grander column that local residents began and then abandoned, because it would have towered over the houses.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Laura Place, the little square at the city end of the street, right by the fountain in the middle. Face along the street towards the Holburne Museum at the far end.

card.hook: Seven separate houses are pretending to be one big palace, and from Queen Square it almost works. John Wood the Elder designed the fronts that way, and the north side is the showpiece.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner where Queen Square Place meets Queen Square. The middle of the square is about 20 m to the east, a few seconds' walk, so face east and look across to the Georgian terraces on the far side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole terrace and the trees in one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier view, and 2x (or 5x if your phone has it) to pick out the doorways and rooflines of one terrace.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stone, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and the stonework both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early on a weekday is likely to be calmest, before the lunchtime office crowds, and the low sun looks lovely on the stone. May is the time to catch the cherry blossom, but skip event days if you want a clear view across the garden.
card.selfie_here: Head into the central garden and stand beside the Beau Nash Obelisk, a popular photo spot and the square's main feature. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone offers it, and turn so the obelisk is over your shoulder. The north terrace, with its seven houses, is another popular spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Queen Square Place corner while you stand by the obelisk, so the terraces fill the background behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Queen Square hosts markets and events, so check access and the official site before you go if you're planning around one.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the seven north-side houses look like a single palace, then step sideways until a gap in the leaves lets the obelisk join them.
card.good_to_know: Queen Square is the first piece of John Wood the Elder's grand scheme, which carries on north to the Circus and the Royal Crescent. Every building around it is Grade I listed. The obelisk was put up by Beau Nash in 1738 for Frederick, Prince of Wales, and it was once taller until a gale in 1815 cut it short.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner where Queen Square Place meets Queen Square. The middle of the square is about 20 m to the east, a few seconds' walk, so face east and look across to the Georgian terraces on the far side.

card.hook: Six locks in a short run, and the water steps uphill like it's late for something. It's a great place to see the repeating lines of the gates all in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon near Rossiter Road, about 170 m west of the locks, and face east. You'll see the stepped locks ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the lock and the water together. From here, try 2x to pick out a single gate or a boat. If you walk closer to the Deep Lock, 0.5x squeezes its depth and the gates into one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the water or a lock gate, then drag the slider to darker if the sky or water looks too bright, so the gates and stonework keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is best, when the light is softer. Midday can put glare on the water, and the towpath may be busier.
card.selfie_here: Take the steps beside the tall gates of the Deep Lock and stand on the grass beside the chamber. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit higher so the gates tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the west end of the Rossiter Road bridge to take your photo while you stand by the Deep Lock below.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay aware of your surroundings, especially near the water's edge and when boats are moving.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line up a gate beam so it points your eye straight to the next lock. Bonus points if a boat drifts into the frame at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: The Deep Lock's chamber is 5.92 metres deep, which makes it Britain's second deepest canal lock. It was created in 1976 when two locks were combined during the canal's restoration. The locks were restored in 1968 by British Waterways staff working with volunteers from the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust, and Abbey View Lock is Grade II listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon near Rossiter Road, about 170 m west of the locks, and face east. You'll see the stepped locks ahead of you.
